items.body:
A key presence on the New York scene over the past 30 years, trumpeter, composer, arranger, and bandleader Steven Bernstein has immersed himself in such a wide array of music with his bands Sexmob, Millennial Territory Orchestra, Diaspora Soul, Universal Melody Brass Band, Spanish Fly, Blue Campfire, and the Butler-Bernstein Hot 9 that his output defies easy categorization. A former member of The Lounge Lizards and Levon Helm’s Midnight Ramble Band, Bernstein has also composed works for film, theater, and dance in addition to doing arrangements for a diverse list of artists, including Lou Reed, Lee “Scratch” Perry, Allen Toussaint, Marianne Faithfull, Linda Ronstadt, Rufus Wainwright, Darlene Love, Mario Pavone, Bill Frisell, and John Lurie. His lengthy list of sideman credits includes appearances on recent recordings by Laurie Anderson (Heart of a Dog), Roswell Rudd (Trombone for Lovers), Mostly Other People Do the Killing (Loafer’s Hollow), Antony and the Johnsons (Turning), and Nels Cline (Lovers). He also continues to perform with Ray Anderson’s Pocket Brass Band, Omaha Diner, and the Kamikaze Ground Crew.

Born in Berkeley, California, Bernstein moved to New York in 1978. By 1990 he had joined The Lounge Lizards, appearing on the group’s 1991 release Live in Berlin (Intuition). Shortly before that, in 1988 he formed the trio Spanish Fly with slide guitarist Dave Tronzo and tuba virtuoso Marcus Rojas. By 1995, producer Hal Willner, a fan of Spanish Fly, enlisted Bernstein as arranger for the soundtrack to Robert Altman’s film Kansas City, which led to collaborations on numerous other Willner projects, including tributes to Bill Withers, Doc Pomus, and Leonard Cohen, among many others.

In 1996, Bernstein formed Sexmob with saxophonist Briggan Krauss, bassist Tony Scherr, and drummer Kenny Wollesen. It remains his primary vehicle for exploring the slide trumpet, a rare instrument that he picked up in a Woodstock guitar shop back in 1977. Over two decades of recording, the group has put their singular stamp on an eclectic list of tunes by the likes of Leadbelly, John Barry, Hoagy Carmichael, Paul McCartney, Duke Ellington, Prince, Kurt Cobain, the Rolling Stones, James Brown, Count Basie, Professor Longhair, and Nino Rota. The group’s latest album, in its 20th anniversary year, is Cultural Capital, the first Sexmob recording to feature all original compositions.

From 1999 to 2008, Bernstein contributed four recordings to John Zorn’s Radical Jewish Culture series on his Tzadik label – 1999’s Diaspora Soul (featuring members of The Lounge Lizards and Sexmob), 2002’s Diaspora Blues (featuring Sam Rivers), 2004’s Diaspora Hollywood (inspired by classic film composers and West Coast cool jazz), and 2008’s Diaspora Suite (a homecoming recorded with Bay Area musicians). Each project combined traditional cantorial songs and elements of jazz, blues, and rock.

Bernstein’s Millennial Territory Orchestra debuted with 2006’s MTO, Vol. 1, which featured large ensemble interpretations of songs by Stevie Wonder, Prince, and the Grateful Dead, as well as Benny Moten and Charlie Johnson and His Paradise Band. They followed with 2008’s We Are MTO, which included renditions of tunes by Fats Waller, Don Redman, Count Basie, and the Beatles. Their 2011 recording, MTO Plays Sly, was a tribute to the music of Sly & The Family Stone and featured the late P-Funk keyboardist Bernie Worrell along with guest vocalists.

In 2012, Bernstein joined up with New Orleans piano master Henry Butler in the retro-flavored Butler, Bernstein and the Hot 9. Their critically acclaimed 2014 Impulse! debut, Viper’s Drag, featured spirited renditions of Fats Waller’s title track along with tunes by Jelly Roll Morton and originals by Butler. The restlessly creative Bernstein continues to juggle several working bands. During a recent residency at The Stone in NYC, he performed with Sexmob, Millennial Territory Orchestra, Spanish Fly, Blue Campfire, and Universal Melody Brass Band.

Bernstein’s latest album is ResoNation Trio/Ultra Resonance (Royal Potato Family). In the liner notes, Bernstein mentions being enchanted by Burning Spear’s Garvey’s Ghost (Island, 1976) back in 1981, only realizing years later that it was a dub version of Marcus Garvey, Burning Spear’s Island release from the previous year. Since then, Bernstein has wanted to record an acoustic jazz trio album and have the results remade as a dub album. The first half of the release, ResoNation Trio, features Bernstein on trumpets, Scott Colley on contrabass, and Nasheet Waits on drums. To challenge himself, Bernstein eschews his main axe (slide trumpet) for this session and instead plays regular valve trumpet, G trumpet, and flugelhorn. The second half is called Ultra Resonance and features the first session tapes remixed and rearranged in dub fashion by longtime producer Scotty Hard, who also adds various keyboards, samples, and percussion to the mix. The former date is as spartan as the latter is dense, yet the two recordings (different though they are in concept and execution), are inextricably linked. I interviewed Bernstein in the summer of 2026, shortly after the release of ResoNation Trio/Ultra Resonance.

* * *

Troy Collins: You’ve been touring with Laurie Anderson the past few years, as documented by the recently released Let X = X (Nonesuch), which features Sexmob as Anderson’s backing band. What has it been like interpreting and rearranging her tunes for Sexmob, especially since Sexmob (in)famously doesn’t typically use pre-arranged tunes and/or setlists? And perhaps more importantly, how did this particular collaboration come about and what is working with Anderson herself like?

Steven Bernstein: Playing with Laurie has been a life-changing experience. She is completely about creation, being in the moment, acting on every inspiration, trying every idea and having fun. Her work ethic is legendary. Her ability to transform an audience is mastery. So being around her and that energy is just a powerful and positive situation. Even though a “show” is basically set once Laurie has decided on it (we are touring a completely different concert, different songs, different stories, different visuals, and a different “theme”) we/she are constantly making changes. Every show day we are at the theatre by 2:00 pm (she gets there at 11:00 am to start working with the lighting director) and we run every piece, whether a new idea comes from Laurie, me, another member of the band, a random sound that makes Laurie say “What’s that? Let’s try that in ‘___’.” Every idea is entertained and often added to the show.

The story of how this all started is beautiful. I’ve been around Laurie and known her at a distance for a long time, but the first time we really worked closely was doing Hal Willner’s Leonard Cohen show in Brighton in 2004. I arranged two songs for her, “The Guest” and “If It Be Your Will.” At Hal’s memorial she wanted to do Lou Reed’s “Gassed and Stoked.” I brought an arrangement that sounded just like the record and we played it through. She turned to me and said, “that sounds great, but I had another idea, I have this new loop” and she starts activating the loop with her violin bowing. It was a very “Laurie-style” loop: rhythmic, sonic, and not in 4/4 time. Tony and Kenny just drop in and start playing. It was grooving and effortless from the first sound. Laurie ended up testing positive for Covid and was unable to play the memorial, but a week later she calls and says how much fun she had playing with us. She said, “I’ve never had that feeling playing music” and that Warners is re-releasing her records and she was thinking of revisiting her older material (which she had never done), and asked would Sexmob play with her? You know my answer.

TC: Since you mentioned him, I’d be remiss to not ask about your years working with Hal Willner. The man’s various artist projects were significant touchstones in my development as a listener. I know he was a big fan of Spanish Fly – is that how you first met? And how did you become his go-to arranger for so many of his projects?

SB: I heard Hal’s Nino Rota record the summer of 1981 while visiting back home in Berkeley. Peter Engelhart, the legendary metal percussion maker played it for me (his daughters are some of my oldest and best friends). It changed my DNA! After that it became a thing. Who is Hal Willner? Where is Hal Willner? I did Night Music with Karen Mantler in 1989. I also played with Carla Bley, Bootsy, and Allen Toussaint on that show. Hal came up to me and said that he was a fan of Spanish Fly, that he’d been coming to our gigs at the Knitting Factory (lurking in the back I’m sure). He gave me his number and said that he would love to help us in any way he could. That led to him producing the first Spanish Fly record (on Knitting Factory records). It is a great Hal Willner production. Hal and I had very similar musical loves and ideas about music, he believed in me and kept offering me amazing opportunities. That led to a 25-year relationship. He could ask me to arrange for Elton John, Bill Frisell, Nick Cave, Lou Reed, Courtney Love, Robert Altman, Marshall Allan, U2 – it was always magic and natural. When I met him, it was pre-internet, and I would keep a pad of paper next to me during our phone conversations. His references could be Ernie Kovacs, Rahsaan, Allan Ginsberg, Martin Denny, Dorothy Parker, Anne Waldman, The Three Stooges, Gregory Corso, Fellini ... I did my best to keep up and learned a lot.

TC: Talking about Willner reminds me that you’ve done arrangements for more people than I can list, and the stylistic variety of artists is staggering. I’m curious if there’s ever been any job you feel you couldn’t or wouldn’t do?

To clarify, the beautiful thing about music is that someone else can take a song that seems unsalvageable and make something new from it that the original author may not have ever suspected was possible. Having just listened to a recent interview with Bill Frisell, I was reminded of his rendition of Madonna’s “Live To Tell,” which transforms what I would consider to be a lightweight pop song into a rhapsodic epic.

You are obviously capable of the same magic, but I wonder, have there ever been offers that you’ve refused based on the material or direction that someone wanted to go with it? Have you ever encountered a song that you felt was simply unredeemable?

SB: Well, there’s a funny story from about 8 years ago, at the beginning of Trump’s 1st term. It was a slow time (as often is the case for freelance workers) and I got an email from someone about arranging/producing some songs. The guy is a Sexmob fan, knows my work with Hal, and he has written some protest songs, tells me he thinks he can get Bono to sing on them, etc. He is not a professional musician, but this is his passion. He also has a vision of a performance piece situation, where the song is played while the listener goes down the “golden elevator” and walks somewhere else. We agree to a fee and he sends me the demo. He is playing rudimentary chords on the piano, and sings one verse, one chorus – it’s about 25 seconds. I call him and ask if there is more, he says no that’s the song. I explain that songs usually have a second or third verse, maybe a bridge, but he says no this is the song. I explain to him that it’s about 25 seconds, and if he wants it to work the way he is envisioning, (going down the elevator and walking) it needs to be at least 3 minutes long. He says, “Well do that Sexmob thing.” I talk to my wife and tell her that I don’t know if I can do this and she says “I thought you said you can make music out of anything.” So, I did and it ended up very cool!

TC: Well then, the obvious follow-up question to that is – did Bono sing on it?

SB: NO. A total pipe dream!

TC: Since we’ve been talking about arranging, I assume nothing is off limits in your own bands regarding your original tunes. Are there any pieces specifically written for say Sexmob, Millennial Territory Orchestra, or Spanish Fly that don’t translate as well from one band to the other, or do you compose your pieces so that any of your bands can perform them?

SB: Each piece is written not only for the band, but specifically for the players in each band. So, there hasn’t been much crossover. There is a piece I wrote as a commission during the pandemic that I played with Sexmob and MTO, but it really worked better as an MTO piece. But the very last phrase (the kicker) of the MTO end of night theme came from a Spanish Fly composition!

TC: Let’s move on to your new album. Your latest release for Royal Potato Family, ResoNation Trio/Ultra Resonance present two very different facets of your artistry – the former title finds you playing on valve trumpet and flugelhorn (instead of the ubiquitous slide trumpet) accompanied by bassist Scott Colley and drummer Nasheet Waits, while the later features Scotty Hard remixing the trio. How did this project come about and when did you first meet and work with Scotty Hard? It seems to me your working relationship with Hard goes all the way back to the very first Sexmob album, 1998’s Din of Inequity.

SB: This project came about because of a grant from the Shifting Foundation. The idea of creating original music with the orchestration of valve trumpet, acoustic bass, and drum set has been a dream of mine for a very long time. This particular vibrational intersection is not widely used, so the unknown possibilities are vast. On a musical/improvisational/technical level it has a very specific set of challenges, and it has taken me this long to feel ready to undertake this long-held desire. Scott Colley and Nasheet were always the musicians I wanted to do this with; I have known them both a long time, and they are veteran masters of spontaneous composition. Another long-held dream has been to create a dub version of an improvisatory instrumental record. I heard Garvey’s Ghost in 1981, and it changed my DNA. Once I started making my own records, I was just waiting for the right opportunity ... and this was it. The trio record is purely conversational and in the moment; back porch music with unlimited harmonic and structural possibilities. The time spent on this record was the decades of playing and writing that preceded it. Ultra Resonance is a mirror image, in that Scott creates his pieces layer by layer, adding and subtracting sounds and rhythms – it takes weeks to build a track.

When I first started playing in The Lounge Lizards with Michael Blake on tenor, Scotty started coming to hang; he was a friend of Michael’s from Vancouver. The first session we did with him was for a Justin Warfield record on Quincy Jones’ label Qwest. It was produced by Prince Paul (I am a huge fan of De La Soul). Scotty wrote the horn chart and engineered. Scotty went on to record and produce the first four Sexmob records. I was already doing fast cuts and dropouts live, but Scotty’s mixes/arrangements shaped the sound of the band.

TC: Having just listened to Sexotica (Thirsty Ear, 2006), your collaborative effort with the production duo known as GoodandEvil (Danny Blume and Chris Castagno), I’m curious how that experience was compared to your similar efforts with Scotty Hard? How does GoodandEvil’s working method differ from Hard’s and what are your thoughts on the different outcomes?

SB: Regarding the two albums/processes – they were fundamentally different as working methods and outcomes. We went into Sexotica (which got a Grammy nomination) with the idea of creating a project that was half acoustic and half electronic. Sexmob went on and recorded all the compositions (two of them being loose jams with input from Danny Blume). Then we did a full day of overdubs with Kenny: wood percussion, metal percussion, bird whistles, and gongs. Then GoodandEvil did their magic. Some pieces skewed more acoustic, some more electronic. The idea was an even balance overall.

With Ultra Resonance Scott was given all the tracks (20 songs). The first track he made, “Titano,” was a piece that’s not on the trio record, but I felt it would be a good piece for Scotty to put his magic on. I figured he would do a “remix” of it, but he rewrote the bass line and created a brand-new piece (natch). After that it was just letting Scott experiment and follow his muse. We had mapped out a series of “zones” we wanted the pieces to be in, but everything Scotty created was totally unexpected. Part of this was the idea of intentional experimentation – on both of our parts. For me it was the idea of the acoustic record, for Scotty it was some new boxes/plug-ins that he had recently received, and the idea of not going back to his tried-and-true techniques. Also, with Sexotica I was not involved in their process, but with Scotty I would hang in the studio once the “track” was created, and was involved in arranging process (Scott claims I had 3 good ideas, I’d say more like 7.6).

As far as my thoughts on the outcomes – two singular recordings that I believe are unlike anything else in the modern recording world. I’m proud of that.

TC: Switching gears slightly (towards acoustic sounds), you’re a fan of vintage horns. I’m assuming that there are certain models you never take on tour and some that you take on the road more frequently? What are the criteria for those distinctions? And what about the slide trumpet? I’m not familiar with anyone else playing one, so where and when did you ever find one?

SB: Vintage trumpets aren’t an issue on the road. I just use the horn best suited for the music. The horn I used touring with Levon Helm was a handmade Chicago Benge from 1947. That was a horn that could project over a five-piece horn section and two electric guitars. It had amazing response and Levon could feel my beat matching his. That’s not what I need with Laurie Anderson!

Regarding the slide trumpet – I found my first horn in a guitar store in Woodstock in 1977 when I was attending Creative Music Studio. When I started Sexmob 30 years ago my old friend (and master repairman) Dick Akright in Oakland (who I met in 6th grade) built the horn I use. It’s one a kind! I’ve collected almost every brand of slide trumpet over the years, though they are not as playable as my horn.

The first horn was $25, at the time (mid-70s) and many trumpet players had one because they were cheap and easily available.

TC: Speaking of Levon Helm, what was it like working with Helm and how did that relationship come about?

SB: This is a long story. I knew Levon had been having “rent party” gigs at the barn. Tony Scherr had done some, and Erik Lawrence did as well. Levon was in danger of losing the barn, as this was a last-ditch attempt to raise some money and also make some music. Erik had invited me to play a few times, and there was a Saturday where I was available (I often did a wedding on Saturday, as I was raising a family, and those gigs paid the bills). Anyway, they mention a few songs Levon might want to do (no Band songs) and said come up early because we might rehearse. We got up there and Levon didn’t come out, so I sat with a boombox and learned a few more songs that Levon “might want to do.” It was a nice chill hang up there, and when it became clear that there was not going to be any rehearsing, I told Erik Lawrence “Don’t play what I play. You just play what you hear, and I’ll play what I hear.” That way we were both free to react to the music. We were playing with Olabelle, and Levon just walked up and got behind the drums. It was the most natural improvisation/spontaneous composition. Levon didn’t know my name, had never seen me before, just smiled at me and told me what he needed with his drum fills. It was magic, and in true Levon form, he put a song from that night on one of his CD’s. Pure improvisation – we had never met!

As far as working with him – it was some of the most magic, swinging, joyous, pure music I have ever had the opportunity to create. He taught me so much about playing in time, playing melody, playing directly from the heart to the people. He was as great and real and no bullshit and smart as you would think from his legendary status. And we had FUN. And he went from almost losing everything to winning three Grammys in eight years!

TC: Speaking of legendary performers, how did you meet pianist Henry Butler, and what was your working relationship with him like?

SB: Another long and beautiful story. In the summer of 1984, I was working with the Flying Karamazov Brothers. We spent two months doing a show at the Goodman Theater in Chicago, and then went on to do a second show at the Olympic Arts Festival in LA. When that was over, they invited me up to the Eugene Country Fair, a legendary hippie festival that was associated with Ken Kesey and the Grateful Dead family. When they asked if I’d like to join them on the Old Time New Age Chataqua tour, a traveling group of “New Vaudevillians” – musicians and environmental activists that toured small communities in the rural Northwest, camping out and putting on shows – that seemed like a better option than returning to my non-air-conditioned fifth story walk up apartment on 109th street in July.

Our first stop was our one actual “gig,” at the Vancouver Folk Festival, and we headed up there directly from the Eugene Country Fair, where we had been enjoying the kind of quality research one would associate with the Grateful Dead Community. As we entered the festival, I heard a sound I was not expecting at a folk festival – a piano player, playing and singing music that seemed like it was completely futuristic, and at the same time playing music that seemed to come from early pre-jazz America. I had never heard anything like this, and at first, I thought my ears and brain were still vibrating from my Country Fair adventures, but it was actually being played, and it was (a pre-Impulse records) Henry Butler. He completely changed my DNA and I became a fan, buying his records when they came out.

When the Kansas City soundtrack record came out on Verve records, it was a time of flowing money in the record business, CDs were selling, and I believe the Bertleman Family had bought the Verve company. In 1995 they organized a cross-country tour with the Joe Henderson Trio, Charlie Haden Quartet West, and the Kansas City All-Stars, which included many Verve artists. I was the musical director of a band that included David “Fathead” Newman, Don Byron, Nicholas Payton, Christian McBride, James Carter, Mark Whitfield, etc.

I had contracted the band but was unable to find a piano player (Gerri Allen and Cyrus Chesnut had done the movie). I contacted seemingly every pianist in NYC who would fit the bill, and none were available, and I was starting to panic. I called Hal Willner to ask his advice and without missing a beat he said “did you call Henry Butler?” And that’s how it all started.

Henry and I were kindred spirits and when the tour was over he told me we would work together again. In 2011 I was doing an “MTO Plays the Early Blues” concert at a summer series in NYC. The promoter, Jay Weisman, asked if I’d like to have Henry Butler play, and I said of course, but where is he? It turned out he had an apartment in Brooklyn, post Katrina. When the concert was over Henry called me and said we should do a show with MTO playing all of his music – that was the birth of Butler Bernstein and the Hot 9 (there were 10 people in the band). As far as my working relationship, he totally trusted my bandleading instincts and arranging, and I was always awed and inspired by the music flowing out of him.

TC: You bring up a salient point. Around the time of the Kansas City soundtrack, there seemed to be a very healthy major label interest in jazz that benefitted musicians of all stripes, even those somewhat on the fringe (James Carter, Don Byron, David Murray, etc.), which to me, evoked the pre-Young Lions era, when major labels signed post-loft jazz artists like Anthony Braxton, Arthur Blythe, and Henry Threadgill.

Much has changed since then. I’m curious what your thoughts are on that phenomenon? How have you adapted to the changing fortunes of the recording business? And what do you foresee for the future?

SB: Well, the beautiful thing is that I have been DIY since the beginning. I think the budget of the first Spanish Fly record (which was on Knitting Factory Records) was 3K, and Hal Willner produced it! I personally have never really had a record contract where I was signed and had a budget. I’ve had a few independent contracts, and records funded by public and private grants. That is the way everything is now, so it’s just the way I’ve always been able to create new things. And that’s what it’s about, creating new things.

TC: In reference to creating new things, I’m curious about your thoughts on live performance versus studio recording. Studio recordings of Sexmob often feature a fair amount of electronic manipulation and remixing, much like Ultra Resonance. What are your thoughts on the difference between purely acoustic performances versus such heavily processed and studio manipulated recordings? Do you vary your approach towards playing depending on the situation?

SB: My feeling is that once Electric Ladyland and The White Album came out, there was no turning back. Even my albums that aren’t “heavily electronically processed” (aka produced by Scotty Hard) feature mixes that are very specific, often times emphasizing certain frequencies, the same way a painter will use certain colors to draw the eye. I believe a record should be a mind-altering listening experience. ResoNation Trio is also a studio record, although one that creates a vision of an imagined acoustic experience. As far as playing, I just do the best I can when the recording light is on!

TC: Let’s go back to those early, heady days. According to your bio, you grew up in the Berkeley area and were friends with Peter Apfelbaum, with whom you regularly attended jazz gigs. There was mention of an “eye-opening gig” by the Art Ensemble of Chicago at San Francisco’s Great American Music Hall. What was it about that particular show that resonated with you?

SB: It was just seeing them live after listening to the records for two years. The magic and visceral-ness of it. There is magic that happens when you are in the room, seeing the musicians and feeling the vibrations, sharing the communion of music. We also met them that night. We were pretty heady. We went to their dressing room and banged out “Nfamoudou-Boudougou” on the door. They were certainly shocked to open the door and see two scruffy teenagers.

They welcomed Peter and me into the dressing room, and that started a relationship that continues to this day (Peter is still in touch with Roscoe). When I moved to NYC I went to see the AEC at the Public Theatre, either late 1979 or early 1980. Now when we went to shows in the Bay Area everyone was dressed hippie funky, so that’s how I showed up, probably in overalls and a t-shirt. I go backstage after the show and am totally self-conscious to be surrounded by well-dressed urban New Yorkers in Kente Cloth and immaculate jewelry. Lester opens up the dressing room door, peeks out at all the “beautiful people” and says “BERNSTEIN get in here!” closes the door, points to the table and says “you can roll a joint, right?” (I could).

TC: Now that’s funny. I certainly remember my one and only time seeing the Art Ensemble of Chicago. It was in Philadelphia, at The Clef Club. Jarman wasn’t touring with them at this point, but it was still magical, ceremonial even.

One group I regretfully never saw was The Lounge Lizards. You were a member of The Lounge Lizards in the 1990s. How did that association come about? And while bandleader John Lurie has had an unusual (to say the least) life and career path since then, I was wondering, do you still have any contact with him?

SB: I have yet another tall tale to tell. It was summer of 1989 and I was touring with Chautauqua again, the same group of people I was touring with when I first heard Henry Butler in 1984. Back then we had answering machines that you called into and used a beeper to retrieve your messages (This is pre cell phones). I was in a small town somewhere, probably Idaho or Montana, and I went to a payphone and checked my messages, and I heard a message from John’s assistant saying to call John up because he was interested in having me join The Lounge Lizards. Needless to say I was beyond excited, because The Lounge Lizards was the “Premiere Band” on the downtown scene.

I call John up and the first thing he says to me is “Do you have a suit?” The next thing he says to me is “you’re not gonna get a lot of solos.” Luckily, the tour was heading to a place of general civilization (Port Townsend) and I was able to put together a tape so John had an idea of what my playing was like, and that September I started rehearsing with the band.

I still talk with John. The most recent project we did together was working on music for his film, that was two summers ago. We did music for Painting with John, and there was an excellent and entertaining episode in season three (I believe) that featured the making of the soundtrack, which really showed the process that we use.

Early on with The Lounge Lizards I started to arrange and transcribe for John, first working on Fishing with John, which led to arranging and conducting soundtracks such as Get Shorty and Excess Baggage. Get Shorty was the summer of 1995, and John and I would spend 12 hours a day together as I transcribed his ideas and put them into notated forms.

TC: I’m glad to hear you’re still in contact with John. Speaking of the 1990s, you recorded four albums in the late 1990s to early 2000s for John Zorn’s Radical Jewish Culture series on his Tzadik label: Diaspora Soul (1999); Diaspora Blues (2002); Diaspora Hollywood (2004); and Diaspora Suite (2008). As a fan of those albums, I’m curious if you ever return to any of those tunes or arrangements?

SB: I’m glad you brought up those records. I love the Diaspora series too. Yes, it lives on. I wrote big band arrangements of some of this music for Arturo O’Farril and the Afro Latin Jazz Orchestra for two different concerts. I arranged a version of “Ani Mamin,” which I recorded with saxophones and valve trumpet on Diaspora Soul, reimagined as a tribute to Eddie Palmer and Conjunto Libre, arranged now for four trombones and slide trumpet. I learned that Barry Rogers, the architect of the New York salsa trombone sound, was raised in Brooklyn and his father and uncle sang with Moshe Kousevvitskey’s choir. Full circle New York history for you. I also recorded a version of “Cha” with Arturo and the Afro Latin Jazz Orchestra. We recorded it during the pandemic, so it's all over-dubbed. “Cha” was inspired by John Zorn’s composing for Masada, and I created an arrangement inspired by Machito. I recently revisited the Diaspora Blues music alongside Arturo O’Farrill, Anat Cohen, and a small version of the Afro Latin Jazz Ensemble. This October at the Stone I'll be premiering a duo version of the Diaspora music with Arturo O’Farrill, so the music lives on, and keeps evolving.

TC: What other musical projects or performances do you have coming up in the near future?

SB: Here are a few upcoming shows:

September 23-29: Laurie Anderson and Sexmob, West Coast Tour and Chicago October 1: Helm Family Ramble in Brooklyn October 2: ResoNation Trio at Tempo, Kingston NY October 28: ResoNation Trio at The Stone October 29: Ultra Resonance at The Stone October 30: Diaspora Special Edition with Arturo O’Farrill at The Stone October 31: Sexmob Kurt Weill Halloween at The Stone

Sexmob Live at Carambolage, Bolzano (the last night of our March 2026 European tour) will be released at the end of the year. It’s our first documentation of the “new sound” of the band with Kenny’s electro drums in the mix.

And more upcoming projects that I’m not quite ready to announce.

items.body:
According to its founder, Eugene Rodriguez, who also sings and plays on the record, Los Cenzontles is a �musical group and non-profit organization, which I founded over thirty years ago.�  As he continues in the album�s liner notes, the group �has a long history of producing projects exploring Mexico�s deep roots and our connections with various traditions that, so far, have included Irish, Louisiana Creole, Cuban, American cowboy, classical, pop, rock, and blues�, the latest of which is
Adios Ke Aloha: Waves of the Same Sea
. Los Cenzontles translates to the mockingbird, or, from its Aztec root word, the bird of four hundred voices. This is a fitting name for the range of musical diversity represented here.
With songs sung in Spanish, Hawaiian, and English, the concept traces back to the legacy of Mexican cowboys who travelled from California to the Hawaiian Islands to wrangle the long-horned cattle introduced there in the nineteenth century. They also brought the guitar. The 16 tracks feature old Hawaiian songs with new Spanish lyrics, old Mexican songs with new Hawaiian lyrics, new compositions, and traditional Americana. Yet it is an entirely cohesive musical package held together by dense arrangements of ukuleles, guitars, Mexican harp, and accordion.
Sonny Lim & David Hidalgo
Besides their distinctive voices, the headline artists Taj Mahal and David Hidalgo provide the gravitas and musicianship that their long and distinguished careers have earned. According to the liner notes, they were the catalysts behind the project and facilitated the choice of songs, arrangements, and played a range of instruments. On vocals they are joined by Hawaiian natives Gary Haleamau, Sheldeen Haleamau, Sonny Lim, and long-time Cenzontles member Fabiola Trujillo.
Deportee
To give a taste of the sessions, included before the traditional �Fishin� Blues� is Taj Mahal teaching the musicians how to play it. Sung by David Hildalgo,  the lovely �A Matter of Time� comes from the 1984 album
Will the Wolf Survive
by his most famous project, Los Lobos. Another standout for me, �Navegar� features a slack string guitar solo reminiscent of Duane Eddie and one of many tasty lap steel turns by Sonny Lim. Their interpretation of Woody Guthrie's �Deportee� moves into social commentary, highlighting the cruel realities of being a migrant worker in America.
Vaquero Paniolo
Recorded over five days, mostly live in one room at the Los Cenzontles headquarters in San Pablo, California, including the talents of some of their academy�s students, the recording has real spontaneity to it. Arrangements are stretched by improvisations, sometimes by several different instruments on a single tune. The project also represents a great spirit of cooperation and diversity of language, culture, age, and gender. It includes the inputs of musical legends, seasoned pros, and amateurs. The wonderfully rich and often stereotyped musical cultures of both Mexico and Hawaii are represented here with the authenticity of lived experience.
Adios Ke Aloha: Waves of the Same Sea
is a worthy addition to Los Cenzontles� important work. Quoting Rodriguez again, �Culture is a fabric within which we are all woven.�

items.body: For an overview of the what, the why, and the where of this music, do read my review of Volume 1 of this series. Essentially, this collection is more of what made Volume 1 so infectious. Yet, what makes this music so fascinating in general, that is, beyond its unswerving ability to fill dance floors, is the fact that these two islands, part of the Paises Africanos de Lingua Oficial Portuguesa (PALOP) regions of the world, are the second smallest African country; Seychelles is smaller. There are only 12 villages on Sao Tom�, lots of rain forest and, not surprisingly, lots of rain. I mention this because one could be fooled into thinking, with music like what�s on offer here, there must have been a music scene larger than there actually was. Not that little was happening, but that less got recorded or released than it might have had there been a city such as Lagos or Nairobi with the studios, labels, and pressing plants to better document it all. The music here, like Volume 1- recorded during Africa�s so-called golden age- is known as Puxa, a complex stew of ingredients from other former African Portuguese colonies mixed with rhythms that, with the help of dancers, can summon spirits or exorcise demons. At least according to some. It�s worth knowing that a 100 years or so ago, the Portuguese banned Puxa dance; it�s also worth knowing they appear to have failed miserably at this silly endeavor. Tucked away in modern Puxa is merengue, Kompas, Soukouss, Benga, and much else. One suspects much of this is coincidental, while other grooves were definitely imported considering both Portuguese rule and the islands� location over the Atlantic from the Caribbean. But don�t be fooled into thinking these two islands don�t have their own thing, as the sounds on this collection show. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s - Pedro Lima Pedro Lima, who has featured in his own Bongo Joe collection, leads a fiery band, complete with choked guitar vamps tussling with a kit drummer as a lead guitar comments from the sidelines on �Sossegado.� Elsewhere, Sangazuza demonstrates what happens when the bass and keys drop out, leaving the drummers and guitars to ride out a groove and drive dancers mad in the process. Check �Sono s� ku� de t�ma� or �Mairo bi cedo� for their ability to place a firm finger on the pulse. Over 15 tracks, the collection shows off multiple guitars weaving and circling one another, with lead and harmony vocals constantly in response, becoming part of the songs� melodic framework. At any given moment, vocals give way as the music unspools and floats on grooves that must have gone on for hours live. Africa Negra�s �Apoi�mos a luta dos nossos irm�os� is one example. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s by Various Artists In general, what�s on offer here, like Volume 1, was recorded at Radio Sao Tom� e Principe (RSTP), often taped in the courtyard outside at night, and released on cassette or occasionally, vinyl. It captures the joy of post-1975 independence and only fizzled out as styles changed and musicians struggled to make ends meet. Yet, take a quick listen to recent RSTP programming, which features musicians such as Babilonia or Calema, and you�ll still hear Puxa rhythms, showing just how potent the music form this two-island nation is on a global level. And Bongo Joe, who have also released two volumes featuring the above mentioned Africa Negra, have given this music the treatment it deserves, with extensive notes on the country�s history, vintage photographs, and band discographies. items.body: A confession to begin: I�ve been a fan of Alison Cotton�s music for quite a while, so the announcement of a new album definitely brought me a frisson of delight. The Gods Laugh certainly doesn�t disappoint, with the same deliciously amorphous feel that�s defined her other work, drawing on folk, the avant-garde, as well as a sense of religiosity to make the music here, possibly best exemplified in �I Am!�, where she set a poem by John Clare, England�s great nature poet, to a transcendent melody over the constant underpinning of a lulling drone. While the playing revolves around her usual arsenal of viola, harmonium, hammered dulcimer, and piano, along with some percussion, on this album she also adds some drums, bass and synthesizer. The music is often improvised and captured in a single take, with an almost mystical, hushed sensibility that seems to reach through time, as with �I Still Know You are Calling My Name,� where the tune could have been plucked from an old folk song. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The centerpiece, however, is �Sprigs of Heather,� with an opening that recalls medieval sacred music that becomes a simple, slowly cascading, piano-led melody. It�s far from the longest track on the album, but a little pearl of perfection that carries the listener away. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The Gods Laugh is a memorial of sorts to Cotton�s father, who died in late 2024. There�s a sense of loss reaching across these tracks, most specifically present on �The Final Harvest,� a solemn piece about her father�s last visit to the allotment he loved so much. It�s suffused with tenderness that extends beyond words. Light and darkness bleed into each other across the music, and moods shift. It�s music that happily stands beyond category, with hints of so many things, but ultimately standing as Alison Cotton music, which might well be all the definition it needs. It will challenge you but also satisfy and move you. What more can you wish from music? Find the artist online. items.body: Those of us who have been digging into Analog Africa�s increasingly formidable releases over the last two decades are well aware of the massive amount of raw, vodun-based Sato and Sakpata-derived funk the label has issued by Benin�s most prolific 1970s-era band, the Orchestre Poly-Ritmo. AA has dropped no fewer than 3 compilations of their heaviest material, as well as a reissue of the band�s first LP, in an effort to give them the international status they deserve. That being said, what might be different about this collection of their music? And who is Antoine Dougb�? Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa As it turns out, Dougb� was a song-conjurer whose mode of musical transfer was slapping his legs in a rhythm known as Cavacha, a groove created by drummer Belobi Meridjo, who was inspired by a train cadence that he worked into a pattern that ultimately spread like a 21st century California wildfire throughout Congolese pop music in the mid-1970s. Dougb�, known as the �Devil�s Prime Minister,� was also a practitioner of vodun who inspired fear in any musician he felt was unsuited to play his music, which is how he landed on working exclusively Poly-Ritmo, as he felt they could nail what he wanted in ways other bands couldn�t. His recording career was brief - 3 albums and a few singles - but as this collection shows, it was potent. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa Because of the era from which this music dates, it�s not surprising that the recording and instrument tones have changed - the guitars have a plastic sheen and synthesizers appear- even if the music remains rooted in the 1970s. Perhaps the influence of the Cuban son is more apparent here than on other Poly-Ritmo collections, especially in the collection�s initial offerings. And yes, Congolese rumba, then shaking all of sub-Saharan Africa to its knees, is present too. �Ma Won Min Towe Leo� is one example. Opening with a bed of synthesizers, the shimmering guitars, tinny, seemingly squeezed dry by the 80s themselves, lock in over relentless high-hat-focused grooves. The guitars finally start firing in different directions midway through, before that synth weaves back in, forming a bed underneath it all. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa �We Tayi Sin Assi Tche� is much more overtly Cuban. With its insistent cowbell, classic, nasal vocal call and response, and tight, repeated guitar figures, its debt to mid-twentieth century Afro-Cuban sons is transparent. Another track, �Djomido Ma Dougbe Tche� rides a groove reminiscent of 70�s-era Franco classic �Liberte.� The pulse is relentless, and the guitar solo repeats a tight repetition of a few notes, driving listeners to ecstasy all the while. However, none of this music is a mere copy of its influences; rather, like so much potent pop coming from the continent at the time, it is a swirl of major influences rendered by local rhythms and vocal phrasing to give it specific identity, in this case, to Benin. Dougb�s musical role on this collection is a bit murky. One of his three albums has a photo of him, fully mic�d behind a collection of hand drums, so perhaps he served as a percussionist/vocalist; this release never explains. He wasn�t a songwriter in the traditional sense. It seems he was more of an instigator and arranger, but his thumbprint was apparently heavy enough to warrant his name on the records he was involved with. Whatever the case, in his brief run as a recording artist, he and Poly-Ritmo produced a handful of driving, Cavacha-inspired grooves that can still wear holes in club floors. Further reading: Petrona Mart�nez - Ancestras (Review) Gnonnas Pedro & His Dadjes - Roi De L'Agbadja Moderne 1974-1983 (Review)

items._cn_summary: Analog Africa 厂牌整理了贝宁乐手 Antoine Dougbé 与 Orchestre Poly-Rythmo 在 1977 至 1982 年间的合作录音。Dougbé 以拍击双腿打出名为 Cavacha 的节奏著称，这种节奏由鼓手 Belobi Meridjo 从火车行进节拍中提炼，后广泛传播于七十年代中期的刚果流行乐中。他本人是伏都教信徒，被称为'魔鬼首相'，只在与 Poly-Rythmo 合作时才感到满意，因此录音生涯虽短仅留下三张专辑与若干单曲，却极具力量。专辑融合了古巴 son 的影响，合成器铺底与闪亮的吉他交织，钹声密集驱动，Congolese rumba 的余波也清晰可辨。整体听感带有七十年代末至八十年代初合成器时代的塑料光泽，同时扎根于贝宁本土伏都传统节奏，是一份展现西非流行乐野史的重要文献。

items.body: Kr�ta , the latest release on Norway's Taragot label, features a Swede and two Norwegians playing interpretations of mainly traditional tunes from their respective countries. Fiddler Mats Ed�n has long been involved in Swedish folk music, as a player, composer and teacher, and in the process exploring and integrating different musical styles and approaches. Tellef Kvifte was in the pioneering Norwegian crossover band Slinkombas in the 1970s and has continued to play a central role in Norwegian folk music, both as a musician and an academic. Most often heard playing the sj�fl�yte , more widely known as a recorder, Kvifte has employed other instruments from outside the Norwegian tradition, in particular the saxophone and bagpipes. His son Knut Kvifte Nesheim , a drummer and composer, has also shown a determination to blur the lines between different musical genres, both in his solo and group projects. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio It comes as no surprise then to find this trio offering a far from conventional take on the tunes they have chosen. While dance tunes may be the source of most of the material here, this feels more akin to chamber music; not that it is remotely classical in style, but in the sense it conveys of three players engrossed in a musically intimate conversation. This is not a performance appropriate for accompanying dancers but might instead be seen as an exploration of hidden possibilities of meaning in the music. In so doing it reveals some of its underlying mystery, including, perhaps, a darker side. Just as in an Ibsen play, where the surface bonhomie, jollity and social nicety can be hiding something more sinister, in Scandinavian dance music there are at times hints of a troublesome undercurrent below the surface. So the decision to open proceedings with �Fossgrimen,� a fiddle tune from Norway's Setesdal valley, is perhaps significant. A fossgrimen is a mythical creature, a kind of water-sprite living in waterfalls from whom fiddle-players were considered to have learned their skills and for that were not universally welcomed, with the fiddle considered to be the devil's instrument. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio Tellef Kvifte takes the lead melody on most tracks but on the Swedish �Polska from Per Myhr,� having played a repeated introductory riff on the sj�fl�yte, with Mats Ed�n providing an amorphous textural accompaniment below and Nesheim adding some quiet tinkling, it's Ed�n who introduces the tune on the fiddle with Kvifte proceeding to play in unison. It's a short track and almost as soon as it gets going things start to fragment and everything grind to a halt.

items._cn_summary: 这是一张由瑞典小提琴手与挪威父子演奏家组成的三重奏专辑，在挪威Taragot厂牌发行。乐评指出，这张专辑对斯堪的纳维亚传统舞曲进行了非常规的重新诠释，将原本用于舞蹈伴奏的曲调转化为类似室内乐的亲密对话形式。三位音乐家各自拥有跨领域背景：小提琴手长期探索瑞典民间音乐的不同风格，挪威演奏家横跨民间、学术与爵士领域，其子则是模糊流派界限的鼓手与作曲家。专辑选择以挪威Setesdal地区与水妖传说相关的小提琴曲开篇，乐评认为这种选择暗示了北欧舞曲表面欢乐之下隐藏的暗流。乐曲中各乐器之间形成层次丰富的纹理互动，既有旋律的齐奏，也有即兴式的碎片化发展，展现了传统素材在当代语境下的多种可能性。

items._genre: experimental electronic / modular synthesis / noise / ambient
items._cn_summary: Modulisme 第146期聚焦法国电子音乐人Poborsk（Patrice Curtillat的个人项目）。作品以模块化合成器为核心，但不追求精致的电子架构，而是刻意拥抱系统的不稳定性：节奏持续偏移，机械化的小动作形成肌理，不同声音层互相碰撞，模块系统被允许以不可预测的方式自行运转。创作路径从早期的盒式多轨录音与吉他出发，逐步走向模块化声音探索。整张作品更接近一种过程性的声音实验而非成品化的电子乐，强调设备自主行为与偶发结果之间的互动关系，为听众提供介于噪音、氛围与电子之间的开放式聆听体验。

items.body: Her grandmother had run out of stories for the night. Go to the cow pen, she told six-year-old Kasiva Mutua , and listen to the secret the black bull is telling the white one. Kasiva went, listened, and returned having heard nothing but a bull sniffing the air. Her grandmother sent her back, told her to listen properly, that the secret was being told right now. The second time, she heard it. Crickets layered on top of each other. Cows breathing in something close to a shared tempo. Wind moving through the trees, laughter drifting from the kitchen. She started humming what she’d heard, then playing it out on her own bed frame, her lap, her chest and cheeks, and from there on anything within reach: pans, spoons, a school desk, a bucket. Percussion belonged to men in the community she grew up in. She took it up anyway, and kept at it until she was one of the only women in Kenya playing it at all, continentally or internationally, and eventually one of the best known. By 25 years old, she was a OneBeat Fellow, and the following year she joined The Nile Project, an East African touring collective she’s stayed with since. Two years later, in 2015, she co-founded MOTRAMUSIC in Nairobi, Kenya’s first all-female percussion collective, taking young women through a year of mentorship in rhythm, composition and performance. She’s also worked with Giant Steps Music and recorded for Coke Studio Africa. TED named her a Global Fellow in 2017, and she has spoken about the drum as a way of telling her own story. In 2020 a OneBeat Accelerator grant let her build Vibe na Queen, an online platform connecting Kenyan women musicians through the pandemic. Her 2022 debut EP Ngewa came after all of that, carrying what the teaching and the touring had put into her playing, and Desturi, her debut album released in February last year, picked up where it left off. Fifteen years, Kasiva says, is how long she has wanted to play WOMEX, hearing it talked about long before she ever stood near its stage, called the World Cup of performances by everyone who had been. On 23 October, in Las Palmas, it happens. She is bringing the album with her, and an open invitation: find her showcase, and come share it. She answered our questions for this year’s Musical Road to WOMEX, on the drum as a way of telling stories, on growing up in a place where it wasn’t meant to be hers, and on what she wants to find on the islands, and put together a playlist exclusively for Rhythm Passport, the tracks hers to choose.  You’ve described the drum as a way of telling your people’s stories. For someone hearing you for the first time, how would you introduce the sound you make now, and where does the voice sit alongside the percussion? Rhythm is a universal language. It’s also everywhere around us. It’s heard, felt, it brings movement (dance, nod, make faces of expression) and evokes emotions. There’s no one who is excluded from rhythm. Children, adults, animals, people of different abilities and backgrounds; we all understand and experience it. We carry rhythm within us throughout our lives, and when the rhythm stops, life ends. For someone hearing me for the first time, I’m a gentle reminder of the joy of having rhythm and how important it is to notice it. The way rhythm sounds and is expressed can vary depending on where we come from, our travels, experiences, and the people and environments we encounter. But in all those variations, is the same foundation; rhythm is something we all carry within us. My sound, then, is something familiar, rooted in East Africa and shaped by nature, my experiences, stories, and the many influences of our African cultures. You learned drumming from your grandmother in a community where the instrument was reserved for men. Looking back, what was the moment you understood that playing it would define your life rather than simply defy a rule? I was inspired by my grandmother’s stories that she told me that taught me to listen to nature. And that way, I started hearing sounds and eventually rhythm. I don’t think there’s an exact moment that stood out, rather a consistent chain of events that led me here. But I can remember a moment I asked myself “Surely, what else in the world can bring me this kind of joy? I LOVE this thing!” WOMEX lands this year in Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, an Atlantic island with its own percussion: the tajaraste, driven by drum and chácaras, the big castanets thought to trace back to the islands’ North African roots. As a percussionist, what are you most curious to hear there? Eeeeeeeverything, man! I wanna hear everything! From the music, to how the children there laugh, and how the water hits the rocks. I’m very curious about the island’s stories too! In a WOMEX line-up full of the world’s traditions, what makes your showcase stand out, and what do you most want people to take from it? My best friend says that there’s nothing as beautiful as watching someone fully immersed in something they absolutely love. There’s something about witnessing that kind of joy; it makes you fall in love with them, and somehow, in the process, you fall in love with yourself all over again. Well… WOMEX is built on unexpected meetings. Are there particular artists, labels or collaborators you’re hoping to cross paths with in Las Palmas? Yes, I’m looking forward to the beautiful connections that will be born out of WOMEX. I’m particularly excited to meet female artists and instrumentalists, some who I have already connected on Instagram, and women working across the music industry. Your drumming is built to pull people in: call and response, bodies moving. A WOMEX audience is mostly music professionals, there to watch and assess rather than dance. How do you win a room like that? Yes, they may be music professionals, but before anything else, they’re human. They are someone’s son, somebody’s daughter. They have kids, They have feelings, emotions, relationships, memories, pain and joy. They’re an audience like any other. Rhythm doesn’t choose where to land or who it belongs to. Even I, myself, cannot control that. It simply does what it does. My role is to play and let it find its way to whoever is listening. Your travels have a way of turning up in your music. Ahead of your first time in the Canaries, is there anything about the islands, their rhythms, their sounds, you’re hoping to come away with? My travels have constantly shaped the person I am becoming. My interactions, experiences and stories all play a big part in the music to come. I’m very curious what this part of my musical journey will look like. In much of Africa the drum has been a man’s instrument, off-limits to women, and you are one of the few who took it up, made a life of it, and spent years bringing other women in behind you. Is there a message you feel especially compelled to carry to an international audience through this showcase? Ah yes. The beauty of our African cultures is that they are deeply complex and constantly evolving. I’ve lived through a time, before mobile phones and the internet, and now I’m living through this period of cultural transition, where we’re all negotiating what we carry forward and how it interacts with the world now. For a long time, the focus was on me being a woman holding a drum. But I think the focus needs to shift from who is playing the instrument to what is being played. I’ve dedicated my life to making sure the rhythms of my people continue to live and travel beyond home, to places where strangers can hear them, dance to them, and perhaps find something of themselves in them. It used to feel significant to be the only woman in the room holding a drum. Today, I’m less interested in that distinction. I’m more interested in the joy of sharing the music, traditions and stories that live within those rhythms, and allowing that to take centre stage. Having moved from percussion into songwriting, production and your own voice, what’s next? New recordings, new collaborations, a direction you haven’t tried yet? I’d prefer to see it as an “expansion of rhythm”. As I evolve, I am finding new ways of expression. I am very open to cultural evolution, and this brings in the aspect of collaboration. Traveling has deeply shaped who I’m becoming and interacting with different cultures adds to my musical DNA. Yes, there’s lots of music to come. Yes, there’s collaborations and yes, there’s many directions I haven’t tried and perhaps are unknown to me just yet. I’m also excited to discover this! If you could write a personal invitation to the people arriving in Las Palmas to come and find your showcase, what would it say? Let me tell you a little story… For about 15 years, as I backed many artists in Kenya and around the world, I always heard this name “WOMEX”. And how it was said to me meant “This is the ‘World Cup’ of performances!” I always wanted to play here. With anyone really. I just wanted to get on this stage. More than 15 years later, it’s going to happen! And with my Desturi, my debut album. WOMEX don’t really understand what they’ve done! They’ve allowed me to live a dream, and by doing so, have now given me permission to take on other dreams… My name is Kasiva Mutua. Find my showcase and come, share my dream come true with me on 23rd Oct, massive Friday night! I’d love to have you there! The bigger the party, the bigger the celebration! Yay! Ahsante! I love you!   Fifteen years of hearing WOMEX talked about end on a Friday night at Plaza del Espigón in Las Palmas. Kasiva Mutua plays there on 23 October, and she's already told the city what she wants from it: the bigger the party, the bigger the celebration!   PLAYLIST: KASIVA MUTUA X RHYTHM PASSPORT   You can find all the previous episodes of Musical Road to Womex HERE   The post Musical Road to WOMEX 2026 – Kasiva Mutua appeared first on Rhythm Passport.
items._genre: world / percussion / folk / global fusion
items._cn_summary: Kasiva Mutua 是来自肯尼亚的女性打击乐手，自幼从祖母的故事中感知万物皆节奏。她打破社区传统对女性的限制，成为少数以打击乐闻名于国际舞台的非洲女性音乐人之一。她参与 The Nile Project 等东非音乐计划，联合创立肯尼亚首个全女性打击乐团体 MOTRAMUSIC，通过 Vibe na Queen 平台在疫情期连接肯尼亚女性乐手。专辑《Desturi》延续了她在首张EP《Ngewa》中积累的巡演与教学经验，将传统东非节奏语汇与个人成长叙事融为一体。整体音乐植根于非洲打击乐传统，同时融入跨文化合作带来的新声音层次，呈现出带有地域文化深度与女性视角的世界音乐面貌。

items.body: Review by kenethlevine — First it was FAIRPORT CONVENTION, but STEELEYE SPAN really planted the flag, and so were followed by worthy extenders in other lands, such as MALICORNE and TRI YANN in France, ANGELO BRANDUARDI and GIAN CASTELLO in Italy, CLANNAD and HORSLIPS in Ireland, MABSANT and PERERIN in Wales, CAPERCAILLIE and RUNRIG in Scotland, OUGENWEIDE and GALAHAD in Germany, MILLADOIRO and SANGRE DE MUERDAGO in Spain, and on and on. Most played a mix of trad/arranged and original/arranged trad style, such that, if you didn't already know, you'd be challenged to distinguish one from the other. They translated ancient poetry and prose into their native language and took liberties with the original melodies when they were known at all. I count myself among those who didn't realize that at least one Finnish group belongs in such select company, but given the breadth of Finnish prog folk, which is like THIS wide, I can't say I'm surprised by the presence or the quality of TARUJEN SAARI ("the island of sagas"), right from this debut.Led by the spirited and technically irreproachable vocals and woodwinds of Kaisa Saari, the hurdy gurdy and sundry from veteran TAPIO MATTLAR, twin violins, and a host of other folk instrumentation, this opening shot straddles all the aforementioned genealogical lines and draws a few of their own. When they choose a tune already well known to the type of people who would listen to this album in the first place, like "The Blacksmith", they give it a fresh spin, in this case it's more potent than the diva-ish LOREENA MCKENNITT rendition or the dirge like versions by STEELEYE SPAN when they were still finding themselves. They even tap the Swedes for the insistent "Margareeta". But the obvious standout here is Sinun Siniset silmasi" (your blue eyes), which merges flawless vocals, organic melody and guest cello.It's worth mentioning that for 30+ years a world beat group named VAARTINA has decorated their own room in trad oriented Finnish folk to an appreciative audience, but TARUJEN SAARI in unison pushes against the 4 (or however many) walls and thus, if not on the island of which they sing, can at least see it from their terrasse.
items._genre: progressive folk / Nordic folk / world music
items._cn_summary: 这张芬兰前卫民谣专辑将传统器乐与编排手法巧妙融合，由Kaisa Saari领衔，辅以手摇风琴、双小提琴及大量民俗乐器。木管与人声交织出富有北欧气息的旋律线，既重新演绎经典曲目（如《The Blacksmith》），也原创具有诗意的作品。专辑将古诗词与传说以芬兰语呈现，与同时代的欧洲民谣运动遥相呼应，但在保留传统根脉的同时加入了前卫元素，拓宽了民俗音乐的表现边界。客座大提琴与有机旋律的结合成为亮点，整体呈现出一种质朴而不失精致的北欧民俗美学。

items.body: Review by bandtutu — Drowning Steps - The Bravery of a Tireless Mind: Book One1. The Angels and the PlaygroundThe Angels and the Playground is an excellent introduction to the album. I really like the way it begins to develop the character's story. One detail I particularly love is the sound of the pencil writing on paper. It may seem like something simple, but it really adds to the immersion in the narrative. Caio's vocals also deserve praise, as they fit the song's concept very well and help convey the emotions behind the story.The first three minutes are beautiful. The acoustic guitar is very well crafted, and the atmosphere at the beginning reminds me of moments from "The Moon Touches Your Shoulder" by Porcupine Tree and "A Pillow of Winds" by Pink Floyd. There is a nostalgic tranquility to this introduction that I really enjoy, with a delicate arrangement that allows each element to find its own space. The song progresses naturally, without rushing, and never becomes tedious.Around 4:15, we get an incredible transition. The guitar riff, accompanied by the keyboards and synthesizers, changes the whole dimension of the composition and creates one of the first major moments of the song. I really like how these elements complement each other. The acoustic guitar picking that comes in here, breaking up the rhythm, also deserves praise.At 6:30, the distorted guitar introduces a section that, although I understand its importance to the narrative and the character's emotional context, buy simply doesn't work for me. I really don't like the riff. I understand the intention behind the change and recognize its purpose within the song, but I feel another approach could have conveyed the same feeling in a better way. It's a very personal criticism, especially because the composition wins me back shortly afterward.At 7:37, another guitar riff comes in, accompanied by the synthesizer, and the result is excellent. The drums also deserve praise, as the changes in the groove give the composition more personality. I really like the bass's rich and distinctive tone, and for me, this combination works so well that it makes up for much of what bothered me in the previous section.At 9:07, after a very striking, almost ghostly break, the song moves into a section that reminds me of "Moonloop" by Porcupine Tree. Even though this is a relatively long passage, it never becomes tedious. The instrumental development keeps me interested and shows the band's ability to sustain extended sections without simply relying on the repetition of the same idea.At 10:47, a riff with a more metal feel begins to emerge. I can't quite define exactly what kind of sound it is, but I really like the change. It's the kind of riff I would even like to write myself, both because of its sound and the energy it carries. Just a few seconds later, at 11:02, another transition completely changes the emotional state of the song. The arrangement takes on a different dimension, setting the stage for one of my favorite moments of the track.The keyboards entering at 11:23 are simply incredible. The piano comes in with a very emotional quality, adding a special sensitivity to everything that had been building up until that point. This section really moved me, especially because of the way the instrument transforms the atmosphere without needing an exaggerated change in intensity. Thiago's work on the keyboards is fundamental here, showing how important his contributions are to the musical identity of both the song and the album.When everything seems to be heading toward a satisfying conclusion, the guitar comes back and creates a sudden shock that, interestingly enough, works very well for me. I don't see this choice as a problem, in fact, I really like the effect it creates.However, my biggest criticism comes right after that, at 12:27, when the previously used riff returns. I feel that bringing it back is unnecessary and slightly hurts the flow of the composition. In my opinion, the song had already found an interesting path toward its conclusion, and I didn't like going back to that idea.Still, I really like the grandiose effect created by the keyboards together with the vocals during the "Then we went up, then we went down" section. The combination has a lot of strength and fits the scale of the narrative, although the repetition of this passage became a little boring for me. The ending of the section, with the guitar delay, works well and sets the stage for the final part of the song.The final section is beautiful. After so many changes in intensity and instrumental passages, the song finally reaches a sense of peace that almost feels like a release. The atmosphere reminds me a lot of "Insurgentes" by Steven Wilson. It also gives me the same feeling of relief I get when "Raider II" ends and "Like Dust I Have Cleared from My Eye" begins on Grace for Drowning. After such a long emotional journey, it feels like you can finally breathe.Despite some choices that don't completely work for me, "The Angels and the Playground" is a very strong opening, with excellent instrumental moments, engaging dynamic shifts, and an atmosphere that contributes just as much to the musical experience as it does to the narrative.------------------------------------2. Fragments of a LifetimeI found this song quite interesting, especially because it takes a very different approach from the previous track. It has this kind of progressive folk-ballad feel, with a very atmospheric arrangement. The keyboard effects also remind me a lot of "Entangled" by Genesis, and I think they fit the song really well.I also really liked the ending, when the song starts to give you the feeling that something is going wrong. It's an interesting choice because it works as a lead-in to the next track, "The Nod", leaving a certain sense of tension in the air.I like the idea behind the lyrics, especially this moment where the character is searching for peace. Overall, it's a simple track, but it works really well within the story of the album. --------------------------3. The NodThe beginning of this song reminds me a lot of Opeth atmosphere. Then a very distinctive guitar riff comes in. I wouldn't necessarily say it's good or bad, but I understand the idea behind it and I think it works.I really like the part around 2:35, when a sequenced drum pattern starts playing in the background. I thought that was a very interesting choice, and it reminds me of some things Wilson has done. The drums also deserve some praise here; they give the song a lot of dynamics and help build that sense of tension without simply making everything heavy all the time.The bass solo is also really good, especially with the character's narration playing in the background. Then the heavy guitar riff from the beginning comes back, and this time I think it really gains more meaning and fits the song very well.I also really liked the synthesizer solo, which brings a different texture to the track. The guitar solo is good as well and works nicely within the composition.Overall, I think the song takes its time to show this depth and develop the idea further.----------------------------------------------4. Waiting for RedemptionThis is easily my favorite song on the album. It starts with a piano in the background and Caio's vocals, which once again deserve a lot of praise. I really like how the song gradually builds along with the lyrics, creating more and more tension as it progresses.The way the song keeps building gives me a strong Neal Morse vibe. I can't really say whether it reminds me more of Transatlantic, Spock's Beard, or his solo work, but there is definitely something about the way the song develops that makes me think of those bands.Around 3:50, a guitar riff comes in and fits the song really well. The effects also deserve a lot of praise here. They manage to create a completely different atmosphere and then return to the previous one in a very natural way, without making the transitions feel forced.This particular riff really reminds me of a riff from the bridge of "Weenie Beenie," from Foo Fighters first album. It's not exactly the same, of course, but the way the riff comes in gives me a very similar feeling.Then, around 5:15, the song goes through a complete change. Once again, it shifts into a darkness and more introspective atmosphere.Shortly after that, the synthesizer solo comes in, and together with the drums, it sounds incredible. Listening to it gives me a really good feeling, almost as if I'm going on a trip. And maybe that's exactly what the character is experiencing in the story as well.Then that heavy riff comes back, this time accompanied by a wah-wah guitar solo, and I absolutely love it. It's really spectacular. The combination of the riff, the guitar tone, and the wah-wah works incredibly well.A new verse then comes in, very well placed, followed by the return of that almost ghostly section, which keeps repeating.My only real criticism is that this final part starts to feel a repetitive. I like the atmosphere it creates, but I think it goes on a little longer than it should.Even so, this is easily the track that stands out the most to me. It has so many great ideas that fit together really well, and the way it moves between different atmospheres while maintaining the narrative is excellent.----------------------------5. Life Handed Me the MapThis is the song that closes the album. It feels like the character is expressing his gratitude for having finally found the path; the "map", that will allow him to reconnect with the fragments of his past.I really like the effects and the atmosphere of the song. There is something very calm and reflective about it, which makes it feel appropriate as the ending of the story.I also really like the detail of hearing him write again at the end of the song, followed by the sound of the book closing. I think it's a great way to bring the album to an end, especially because the sound of the pencil writing appeared earlier in the story. It gives the whole thing a feeling of closure, almost as if we've just finished reading the character's story ourselves.--------------Overall Opinion on the AlbumFor me, this is a work that shows how much the band has matured, both in their songwriting and in the way they tell their story. I really enjoyed the songs, especially the way the album manages to create different atmospheres and make them work within the narrative.The main highlights for me were The Angels and the Playground, The Nod, and especially Waiting for Redemption. Overall, this is an album that really surprised me and shows how much Drowning Steps has evolved. It's a record I definitely plan to listen to over and over again, because I feel like there are still a lot of details to discover.-----------My Ratings:4,3/5 8,6/10Congratulations for this excellent work.Caio Claro / vocals, acoustic guitar (1), guitars (2,5), Arrangements and Sound ManipulationFabricio Mendon�a / drumsLeonardo Gon�alves / bassMarcos Duran / guitars (1-4)Tiago Pierucci / keyboards, synthesizers, effects, organ, piano, Wah-Wah guitar (2), backing vocals (4), Arrangements and Sound ManipulationRobin Peachey / vocals (1)La�s Gonzalez / vocals (2)Erlend Viken / vocals (3)

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以叙事性极强的概念构建开场，首曲便展现出对氛围与情绪层次的高度敏感。开篇的铅笔书写声效、原声吉他拨弦与怀旧的宁静感营造出强烈的沉浸感，编曲留白恰到好处使每个声部各得其所。中段通过吉他riff与键盘合成器的递进展开，频繁的段落转换展现乐队对长篇器乐铺陈的控制力，鼓点律动变化与贝斯音色亦为整体增添个性。评论者特别提到某些riff虽具叙事意图但执行效果欠佳，另一些则以金属质感带来惊喜。整体而言，这是一张在渐进摇滚框架内积极探索情绪叙事与器乐张力的作品，与实验/前卫听感有交集，但核心仍属渐进摇滚范畴。

items.body: I had hoped to be seen by you Unbroken gaze like a sweet arrow Could you ever feel my eyes on you Bathing you in my desire Desire has a way of making the body speak before the mind has decided what to say: flushed cheeks, an aching chest, the unreasonable hope that somebody might feel a glance from across the room. In the video for Sacred Hearts, Gloria de Oliveira takes those private sensations onto the streets of Hamburg’s St. Pauli district, where barroom lamps, photo-booth portraits, and the company of women give longing somewhere to live. The song’s burning heart finds a fitting companion in the red lights overhead, while affection passes between its subjects through looks, laughter, and the small pleasure of being together. The Berlin-based German-Brazilian musician and visual artist shares the video for the third single from her forthcoming album The Lying Swans, due October 30, 2026, through La Double Vie and Cargo Records. Produced by Randall Dunn, whose work includes records with Anna von Hausswolff and Marissa Nadler, Sacred Hearts considers the exhilaration and anxiety of giving yourself over to another person, particularly when the body seems to have made that decision ahead of you. The opening guitar figures carry an almost medieval character, joined by bright, percussive tones with the delicacy of a hammered dulcimer. Matt Chamberlain’s drumming briefly suggests the forward motion of Kate Bush’s Running Up That Hill before settling into the song’s own gait. Deep resonant strings lend the arrangement weight, while synthesizers soften its edges and extend its peculiar, old-world atmosphere. The tones and melody evoke a folk ballad like Nick Cave’s The Weeping Song, with the spaciousness of a Western just beyond the song’s antique ornamentation. De Oliveira sings into that space with a delicate quiver that evokes Elizabeth Fraser, with a classical poise softened by the intimacy of her delivery. Lennard Zander’s acoustic, electric, and 12-string guitars trace fine melodic lines without disturbing the vocal’s tenderness; Arjan Miranda anchors the arrangement on bass, while de Oliveira, Dunn, and Úlfur Hansson add layers of synthesizer. The music leaves her exposed yet almost weightless, as if every declaration of love might tip her toward losing her footing. The lyrics measure desire through its physical symptoms, moving from fever and sleeplessness toward the hope contained in a hand’s touch. To be seen becomes as urgent as to be loved, and the repeated attempts to contain that feeling only reveal its scale. Yet, the song’s title draws on an image de Oliveira has carried since childhood, joining religious devotion to the unruly sensations of romantic attachment. “The Catholic image of Christ’s Sacred Heart – a heart literally engulfed in flames – has struck me since childhood.” “Of course it’s meant to symbolise God’s boundless and passionate love for mankind – however, as John Keats once wrote, ‘I am certain of nothing but of the holiness of the heart’s affections, and the truth of imagination’. And how does it feel to give yourself over to that affection and desire despite fear? With this song, I wanted to capture these seemingly contrasting sentiments.” Shot and directed by award-winning Turkish filmmaker Seda Kaçak, and edited by de Oliveira, the video stars London actress Mona Najma alongside Eva Rogalla. Kaçak follows the women through St. Pauli in handheld close-ups, catching them sharing drinks, posing for photo-booth pictures, and moving between daylight streets and richly coloured interiors. Superimposed faces and starbursts around the lights give these ordinary pleasures an enchanted quality. Conceived as a homage to the bond between women, the film offers an affectionate counterpoint to the song’s solitary ache: companionship makes room for feelings that can otherwise become overwhelming. Watch the video for Sacred Hearts below: A classically trained singer whose acting work includes Babylon Berlin and Christian Petzold’s Undine, de Oliveira released music with the darkwave and synthpop duo lovespells before her 2020 debut album Fascination. Her 2022 collaboration with David Lynch’s longtime sound designer Dean Hurley, Oceans of Time, followed through Sacred Bones. Across those releases, she has explored dream pop, ethereal wave, ambient music, and the influence of her Brazilian roots, alongside work for theatre, film, and London Fashion Week. Recorded in Iceland, New York, and Berlin, The Lying Swans extends those interests across nine songs concerned with trauma, perception, and the difficult return of trust. Its title invokes the myth of Leda, while its literary references include John Keats, Emily Brontë, Anne Sexton, and Milton’s Paradise Lost. Within that broader examination of love and illusion, Sacred Hearts holds open the possibility of affection despite fear. Listen to Sacred Hearts below or via streaming services, and pre-order The Lying Swans here. The album is out October 30, 2026, on digital, vinyl, CD, and cassette. items._cn_summary: Gloria de Oliveira 是常驻德国的巴西裔音乐人与视觉艺术家，新单曲《Sacred Hearts》作为专辑《The Lying Swans》的第三支单曲发布，由曾与 Anna von Hausswolff、Marissa Nadler 合作的制作人 Randall Dunn 操刀。歌曲探讨欲望如何在意识介入之前便已占据身体，以发烧、失眠等生理感受度量暗恋的烈度，MV 将这种私密体验延伸至街区酒吧、照相馆与女性友伴之间。音乐上，开场吉他带有中世纪质感，锤击扬琴般的清脆打击音色与 Kate Bush 式律动交织，深沉弦乐铺底，合成器柔化棱角，整体氛围接近 Nick Cave 民谣谣曲的旧世界气质。De Oliveira 的声线脆弱颤抖，演唱在袒露与失重之间游走。圣心意象将宗教虔诚与浪漫冲动并置，体现其童年延续至今的审美脉络。La Double Vie 与 Cargo Records 为独立发行。
